newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Chidambaram--liberal with political skill.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram--liberal with political skill.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, lauded for breathing new life into flagging economic reforms, has put his free-trade stamp on a coalition government backed by communists.
A Harvard-educated liberal, Chidambaram, 51, was one of the architects of India's six-year-old reforms programme.
But the full measure of his commitment to a more open economy and his political acumen was never more apparent than when he presented the government's budget plan to parliament on Friday.

"Chidambaram pulls off the impossible," the Indian Express newspaper said after the bespectacled minister cut corporate and personal tax rates and slashed import duties in the budget for the 1997/98 year starting on April 1.

Twice commerce minister under former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao who ruled from 1991 until last May, Palaniappan Chidambaram joined hands with the then finance minister Manmohan Singh to propel reforms forward.
The government swept away a battery of restrictions on trade and business in India's decades-old protected economy.
Chidambaram reluctantly resigned in 1992 after admitting his wife had unwittingly invested family funds in a company under investigation in India's biggest financial scandal.

The suave Chidambaram came back in 1995 and resigned again in April 1996 after his Congress party, then headed by Rao, forged a controversial regional electoral alliance in his southern state of Tamil Nadu.
A defiant Chidambaram helped to float a rival regional party, the Tamil Maanila Congress, and won a seat in parliament in the general election held in stages in April and May 1996.

His party is allied with Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front, a coalition of regional, left and centrist parties which formed a minority government with the support of Congress after inconclusive polls.
Chidambaram, who sports neatly oiled hair and a crisp, starched white wraparound cloth "dhoti", is a quick-witted -- and often harsh -- advocate of economic liberalisation.
A lawyer from the southern city of Madras, Chidambaram studied business management at Harvard University in the United States before joining the Congress Party in 1969.

He first joined the government in 1985 as a junior minister in the commerce ministry, later moving to the personnel ministry and the home (interior) ministry under the then prime minister, Rajiv Gandhi.

When Rao reinstated him in a February 1995 cabinet reshuffle, Chidambaram unleashed a new series of trade reform policies. He sought wider market access for Indian goods and urged businessmen to promote Indian brands overseas. He also pledged to dismantle all tariff barriers by the year 2000.

A tireless defender of Rao's liberalisation programme, which critics say ignores the poor and favours big foreign firms, Chidambaram unabashedly wooed foreign investment and supported privatisation of loss-making state-owned firms.

In the new budget, Chidambaram deftly doled out support to targeted interest groups, keeping populists in Deve Gowda's cabinet from rising up against the plan's overall thrust which will expose many Indian firms to greater foreign competition.

The accolades prompted comparisons with Manmohan Singh, considered the driving intellectual force behind the reform movement. Some commentators said Chidambaram had tread where Singh had not dared venture.
But Chidambaram himself was loath to draw a comparison. Asked to comment on the enthusiastic response to his budget, he told Reuters: "Let us see what happens in coming weeks."
Born into a wealthy family of textile barons on September 16, 1945, Chidambaram is married to Nalini, a lawyer. They have one son.
